## Overview of Dataset

We have chosen a patient survival prediction dataset from Kaggle. Each row is an ICU stay, and the binary outcome variable `hospital_death` is whether the patient died during their hospital stay. The dataset has columns regarding the patient's demographics, how they were admitted to the ICU, vital signs and lab results from their first hour and first 24 hours in the ICU, and chronic conditions.

## Business Question

The question we hope to answer with this data set is “Which patient characteristics available in the first 24 hours of ICU admission predict in-hospital mortality, and can they help a hospital prioritize ICU resources?”. This would be helpful to the hospital because ICU beds, staff and equipment are limited and expensive, and knowing which patients are most likely to die within the first 24 hours lets the hospital direct those resources to the patients who need them most. It also helps managers plan staffing and beds, and gives the care team time to talk with families about goals of care.

## Exploratory Data Visualizations

To get a sense of what is related to in-hospital death, we started with a few plots of the raw data.

```{r}
# Load the raw dataset for exploration
raw <- read.csv("patient.csv")

# Figure 1: share of patients who died in each age group
# cut() splits age into 10-year bins, and tapply() takes the mean of hospital_death in each bin
age_group <- cut(raw$age, breaks = c(15, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90))
death_by_age <- tapply(raw$hospital_death, age_group, mean)
barplot(death_by_age,
        col = "firebrick",
        xlab = "Age Group",
        ylab = "Proportion Who Died",
        main = "Figure 1: In-Hospital Death Rate by Age Group")
```

Figure 1 shows the death rate climbing steadily with age, from about 3% for patients 30 and under to about 13% for patients in their 80s.

```{r}
# Figure 2: death rate by GCS motor score, split by whether the patient was ventilated
# GCS motor score runs from 1 (no movement) to 6 (follows commands)
death_by_gcs <- tapply(raw$hospital_death,
                       list(raw$ventilated_apache, raw$gcs_motor_apache), mean)
barplot(death_by_gcs,
        beside = TRUE,                       # draw the two groups side by side
        col = c("navy", "firebrick"),        # 1st = not ventilated, 2nd = ventilated
        xlab = "GCS Motor Score (1 = No Response, 6 = Obeys Commands)",
        ylab = "Proportion Who Died",
        main = "Figure 2: Death Rate by GCS Motor Score and Ventilation")
legend("topright",
       legend = c("Not Ventilated", "Ventilated"),
       fill = c("navy", "firebrick"))
```

Figure 2 shows that less responsive patients die far more often: about 35% at a motor score of 1 versus about 5% at a score of 6. At every score, ventilated patients die more often than those who are not ventilated.

```{r}
# Figure 3: death rate by where the patient was admitted to the ICU from
src <- raw$icu_admit_source
src[src == ""] <- "Unknown"                  # label blank sources so they show up in the plot
death_by_src <- sort(tapply(raw$hospital_death, src, mean))
par(mar = c(5, 13, 4, 2))                    # widen the left margin so the labels fit
barplot(death_by_src,
        horiz = TRUE, las = 1,               # horizontal bars with readable labels
        col = "navy",
        xlab = "Proportion Who Died",
        main = "Figure 3: Death Rate by ICU Admission Source")
par(mar = c(5, 4, 4, 2))                     # reset margins
```

Figure 3 shows that patients coming from the operating room die at only about 4%, likely because many are planned surgeries. Patients transferred from another ICU, another hospital, or a hospital floor die at about 13 to 14%, roughly three times as often.

## Summary Statistics

```{r}
patient <- read.csv("patient.csv")

str(patient)
summary(patient)

# How common is the outcome?
table(patient$hospital_death)
round(prop.table(table(patient$hospital_death)), 3)

# Average of key predictors for patients who survived (0) vs. died (1)
key_vars <- c("age", "bmi", "pre_icu_los_days", "d1_heartrate_max", "d1_sysbp_min",
              "d1_spo2_min", "gcs_motor_apache", "ventilated_apache", "elective_surgery")
round(aggregate(patient[, key_vars], by = list(hospital_death = patient$hospital_death),
                FUN = mean, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
```

The data has 91,713 ICU stays and 85 variables. Only 8.6% of patients died in the hospital, so the outcome is imbalanced. A model that predicted "survived" for everyone would already be about 91% accurate, so we look at sensitivity and kappa rather than accuracy when evaluating the model.

The typical patient is 65 years old and reaches the ICU within a few hours of arriving at the hospital. Compared to survivors, patients who died were older (68 vs. 62 on average), had lower minimum blood pressure and oxygen levels on day 1, and were more than twice as likely to be ventilated (67% vs. 29%). 

## Data Cleaning

```{r}
# Remove unique identifier columns and the empty unnamed column
patient$encounter_id <- NULL
patient$patient_id <- NULL
patient$hospital_id <- NULL
patient$icu_id <- NULL
patient$X <- NULL

# The APACHE IV death probabilities are already a prediction of our response variable
patient$apache_4a_hospital_death_prob <- NULL
patient$apache_4a_icu_death_prob <- NULL

# The APACHE diagnosis codes are IDs, not real numbers, and apache_2_bodysystem repeats apache_3j_bodysystem
patient$apache_2_diagnosis <- NULL
patient$apache_3j_diagnosis <- NULL
patient$apache_2_bodysystem <- NULL

# Blank categorical values become their own "Unknown" level, then convert to factors
cat_cols <- names(patient)[sapply(patient, is.character)]
for (v in cat_cols) {
  patient[[v]][patient[[v]] == ""] <- "Unknown"
  patient[[v]] <- as.factor(patient[[v]])
}

# Fill missing numeric values with the column median
colSums(is.na(patient))
num_cols <- setdiff(names(patient)[sapply(patient, is.numeric)], "hospital_death")
for (v in num_cols) {
  patient[[v]][is.na(patient[[v]])] <- median(patient[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)
}
sum(is.na(patient))

# Create dummy variables for categorical data (drop the intercept column so each factor has a reference level)
patient_d <- as.data.frame(model.matrix(~ ., data = patient)[, -1])

str(patient_d)
```

Cleaning choices:

- We removed the ID columns (`encounter_id`, `patient_id`, `hospital_id`, `icu_id`) and the empty column `X`, since they say nothing about whether a patient survives.
- We removed the two APACHE IV death probabilities. They are already a prediction of death, so including them would leak the answer into the model.
- We removed the APACHE diagnosis codes because they are ID numbers for hundreds of diagnoses, not real quantities, and kept the body system grouping instead. `apache_2_bodysystem` repeats `apache_3j_bodysystem`, so we dropped it too.
- Blank values in the categorical columns became an "Unknown" level, and those columns were converted to factors.
- Every patient is missing at least one lab or vital sign, and `glm` drops any row with a missing value, which would have thrown out about 31% of patients. We filled missing numeric values with the column median instead.
- We created dummy variables for the factors so the data is ready for the train/test split.

## Regression Model

### Splitting the Data

We split the data into a 70% training set and a 30% test set, so the model is judged on patients it has never seen.

```{r}
ratio <- 0.7
set.seed(12345)
train_rows <- sample(1:nrow(patient_d), ratio*nrow(patient_d))

patient_train <- patient_d[train_rows, ]
patient_test <- patient_d[-train_rows, ]

# The death rate should be similar in both sets if the split is fair
mean(patient_train$hospital_death); mean(patient_test$hospital_death)
```

The death rate is about 8.6% in the training set and 8.7% in the test set, so the split is representative.

### Logistic Regression

Logistic regression is used when the outcome is binary, like died or survived. Instead of predicting a number directly, it estimates the probability that each patient falls in the "1" group, using a curve that always stays between 0 and 1. Each coefficient shows how a variable shifts the odds of the outcome while holding the others constant. 

This lines up directly with our business question. The coefficients answer the first part, which characteristics predict in-hospital death (the why), and the predicted probabilities answer the second, since a hospital could flag patients above a chosen risk level in their first 24 hours and give them priority for ICU staff, monitoring and beds.

```{r}
logmodel <- glm(hospital_death ~ ., data = patient_train, family = "binomial")

summary(logmodel)
```

A positive coefficient means a variable raises the odds of dying, and a negative one lowers them. The strongest findings:

- Ventilated patients have about 2.2 times the odds of dying (coefficient 0.77).
- Metastatic cancer raises the odds about 2.3 times (0.83), and cirrhosis about 1.8 times (0.56).
- Every 10 years of age raises the odds by about 33% (0.029 per year).
- Each one-point increase in GCS motor score lowers the odds by about 19% (-0.21).
- Elective surgery (-0.87) and admission from the operating room (-0.67) lower the odds, while transfers from another ICU (0.61) or hospital (0.34) raise them.

These match what we saw in Figures 1 to 3. Diabetes has an unexpected negative coefficient (-0.21), which likely reflects that diabetic patients are often admitted for problems that are easier to treat rather than diabetes being protective. Some variables, like minimum systolic blood pressure, are not significant because they overlap with other severity measures. We plan to try backward stepwise selection in a later deliverable to remove these.

### Test Data Prediction and Confusion Matrix

```{r}
# Evaluate on the test set. Only ~9% of patients die in the hospital, so a 0.5 cutoff misses
# most deaths (sensitivity ~25%). A 0.2 cutoff gave the highest kappa of the cutoffs we tried.
library(caret)
test_prob <- predict(logmodel, patient_test, type = "response")
pred_bin <- ifelse(test_prob > 0.2, 1, 0)

confusionMatrix(as.factor(pred_bin), as.factor(patient_test$hospital_death), positive = "1")

#m1 <- step(logmodel, direction = "backward")
#summary(m1)
```

The model correctly flagged 1,342 patients who died (true positives) and correctly cleared 23,240 who survived (true negatives). It missed 1,059 deaths (false negatives), which are the costly errors because the care team gets no warning. It also flagged 1,873 patients who survived (false positives), which costs some extra monitoring but is far less harmful than a missed death. The more useful numbers are sensitivity (56%), meaning the model catches a little over half of all deaths, and specificity (93%), meaning most survivors are not flagged. 

This shows the dataset is viable: information from the first 24 hours does separate high-risk patients from low-risk ones. The model still misses 44% of deaths, so in later deliverables we will try to raise sensitivity with variable selection, nonlinear terms and interaction effects.

## Appendix: Previous Dataset (Auto Insurance Claims)

We first tried an auto insurance claims dataset, but it only had 11 unique cars, so the vehicle columns could only add 10 independent predictors and the model's test AUC was about 0.60. This code is kept for reference and is not run.

```{r, eval=FALSE}

claims <- read.csv("claims.csv")

# Remove unique identifier columns
claims$policy_id <- NULL

# Every vehicle column is fully determined by `model`, and there are only 11 unique cars.
# That means all vehicle columns combined can only carry 10 independent pieces of information,
# so including more than that is perfectly collinear and gives NA coefficients.
# Drop `model` and greedily keep vehicle columns (in priority order) as long as each one
# adds new information. Numeric/binary columns come first since they use only 1 degree of freedom each.
vehicle_cols <- setdiff(names(claims), c("subscription_length", "vehicle_age", "customer_age",
                                         "region_code", "region_density", "claim_status"))
cars <- unique(claims[, vehicle_cols])

priority <- c("ncap_rating", "airbags", "displacement", "gross_weight", "length", "width",
              "turning_radius", "cylinder", "transmission_type", "is_esc", "is_tpms",
              "is_parking_sensors", "is_parking_camera", "is_brake_assist", "is_front_fog_lights",
              "is_speed_alert", "is_adjustable_steering", "rear_brakes_type")
X <- matrix(1, nrow(cars), 1)
keep_vehicle <- c()
for (v in priority) {
  X_new <- cbind(X, model.matrix(as.formula(paste("~", v)), cars)[, -1, drop = FALSE])
  if (qr(X_new)$rank == ncol(X_new)) {
    X <- X_new
    keep_vehicle <- c(keep_vehicle, v)
  }
}

claims[, setdiff(vehicle_cols, keep_vehicle)] <- NULL

# region_density has a 1:1 mapping with region_code, so keep only region_code
claims$region_density <- NULL

claims_d <- as.data.frame(model.matrix(~ ., data = claims)[, -1])

set.seed(12345)
claims_train_rows <- sample(1:nrow(claims_d), 0.7*nrow(claims_d))
claims_model <- glm(claim_status ~ ., data = claims_d[claims_train_rows, ], family = "binomial")
summary(claims_model)

```
